chunks: "I'd start by asking how many requesters there are, whether a grant lasts one cycle or until the transfer finishes, and whether I need fairness or just priority.
The simplest arbiter is fixed priority. Requester zero always wins if it's asking, otherwise requester one, and so on.
In RTL it's just a priority encoder, and there's a neat one-liner: the grant is the request vector AND its two's complement negation, which isolates the lowest set bit.
It's tiny and fast, but a low-priority requester can starve if the high-priority ones keep asking. For fairness I'd use round-robin.
I keep a mask of requesters that haven't been served this round.
If any masked request is active I pick the highest priority among those; otherwise I pick from the unmasked requests.
After a grant I update the mask to cover only the requesters above the one that just won. That guarantees that with N requesters, nobody waits more than N minus 1 grants.

Beyond that there's weighted round-robin for bandwidth shares, matrix or least-recently-used arbiters that track pairwise priority, age-based arbiters that serve the oldest request for bounded latency, and time-division schemes with fixed slots for hard real-time guarantees.
The trade-off is fairness and latency guarantees against logic cost and timing.
I'd also check invariants: grant is one-hot or zero, a grant only goes to a requester, and I'd verify no starvation in round-robin with a test."
